blocks.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
blocks.text: DFS explores as far down a branch as possible before backtracking to explore other branches, using a stack to manage the nodes to be explored.

items: Start from the root node and push it onto the stack.
Pop a node, process it, and push all its unvisited neighbours onto the stack.
Repeat until the stack is empty.

blocks.text: DFS suits puzzles such as mazes: it follows one path to the end and backtracks at a dead end. Its time is O(V + E), like BFS. DFS is more memory-efficient for deep graphs, while BFS is more suited to shallow graphs.

blocks.alt: Top left: merge sort splitting [14, 7, 3, 12] into halves and single items and merging them into [7, 14], [3, 12] and [3, 7, 12, 14]. Top right: three rows of the sorted list 21 34 43 57 66 78 showing a binary search for 78 with middle values 43, 66 and 78. Bottom left: a tree with root 0, children 1, 2, 3 and grandchildren 4, 5, 6, 7 with BFS and DFS orders. Bottom right: notes on greedy, dynamic programming, backtracking, sorting and searching.
blocks.caption: Merge sort, binary search, BFS and DFS (original diagram after topics 3.5 to 3.7).
blocks.long_description: Merge sort divides [14, 7, 3, 12] into [14, 7] and [3, 12], then into single numbers, and merges them back as [7, 14] and [3, 12] and finally [3, 7, 12, 14]. Binary search for 78 in 21, 34, 43, 57, 66, 78 checks the middle value 43, which is smaller, so it keeps the right half; the next middle value 66 is also smaller, so it keeps the right half again and finds 78 at index 5 in three steps. On a tree with root 0, children 1, 2 and 3, and grandchildren 4 and 5 under 1, 6 under 2 and 7 under 3, BFS visits level by level, 0 to 7 in order, while DFS goes deep first: 0, 1, 4, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7.
